question: According to a study by Parliament’s CULT Committee, job precarity and difficulties in accessing social security are serious issues in the cultural and creative sector. The study attributes this precarity to, primarily, the lack of a clear uniform definition of the various job profiles, coupled with a lack of recognition of the specific nature of much creative and cultural work. In view of this: What steps will the Commission take to address job precarity in the cultural sector?
answer: In its reply by letter of 21 February 2024 (1) to the European Parliament resolution on an EU framework for the social and professional situation of artists and workers in the cultural and creative sectors (2023/2051(INL)), the Commission shared the Parliament’s concerns and informed of past and planned actions. Analytical work on artists’ working conditions has been carried out.

The Commission also facilitated the work of an Open Method of Coordination Group. Recognising the important role of the cultural and creative sectors, the Commission will organise a High-level Round Table with relevant stakeholders in 2024 to explore ways forward to address the needs of the sectors.

Under the EU Work Plan for Culture 2023-2026 (2), yearly thematic workshops with Member States on artists’ working conditions will take place, starting in May 2024. The Commission will assess existing gaps in the application of EU rules in relation to the employment situation in these sectors together with national experts and social partners and will invite them to consider further solutions.

The Commission will work with the Member States to enhance the enforcement of occupational health and safety rules, gather evidence on undeclared work jointly with the European Labour Authority, and facilitate mutual learning on social protection aspects.
